# Arrival Alerts User Guide

## What are arrival alerts?

Arrival alerts notify you when a vessel reports a new position or changes its estimated arrival time. You stay informed about incoming traffic without having to check the system constantly.

## Getting started

To use arrival alerts, you choose which vessels you want to monitor and when you want to be notified. Each alert is customized to your workflow.

### Setting up an alert

1. Select the vessel or vessels you want to track.
2. Choose your notification method: email, SMS, or another system.
3. Set the timing for when the alert should fire.
4. Save your alert.

You can create multiple alerts for the same vessel if you need notifications through different channels or at different times.

## Timing options

You control how close to arrival you want to be notified. Choose one of these intervals:

- **24 hours before arrival** — Get early warning to prepare berth and crew.
- **6 hours before arrival** — Notify teams when the vessel is close.
- **1 hour before arrival** — Final confirmation before the vessel reaches the berth.
- **On berth** — Receive an alert the moment the vessel arrives at its assigned berth.

## Notification methods

**Email and SMS** are sent directly to you. The message includes the vessel's ID, what changed (position update or revised arrival time), and the new estimated arrival time in UTC.

**Alerts to another system** work if your organization uses external logistics software or automation tools. Instead of sending you a message, Harbourlight sends the alert to a URL that your system provides. The alert arrives as a structured message containing the vessel ID, alert type, arrival time, and a signature for security.

### Setting up delivery to another system

Provide Harbourlight with a URL where your system will receive the alert. Your IT team can give you this address if you're not sure what it should be.

Harbourlight will send the alert as a structured message. Your system should verify the signature using a shared secret that you set up during configuration. This ensures the alert genuinely came from Harbourlight and wasn't altered in transit.

## Delivery reliability

Harbourlight makes multiple attempts to send alerts to another system. If the first attempt fails, it waits longer between each try, up to 5 attempts total. If all attempts fail, the alert is logged and remains visible in your alert history for 30 days so you can review what happened.

For email and SMS, delivery is typically immediate. Check your spam folder if you don't receive an SMS or email alert.

## Quiet hours

You can set quiet hours so alerts don't arrive during times when you don't want notifications — overnight, lunch breaks, or shift changes.

During quiet hours:
- Email and SMS alerts are held and sent when quiet hours end.
- "On berth" alerts are always sent immediately, regardless of quiet hours.

This ensures you never miss a vessel arrival at your berth, even if quiet hours are active.

### Managing quiet hours

1. Go to your user settings.
2. Set your quiet hours by time of day.
3. Save your preferences.

Quiet hours apply to all your alerts. If you need different quiet hours for different alerts, create separate notification profiles.

## Viewing alert history

All sent alerts and failed deliveries appear in your alert history. You can search by vessel, date, or status. This record helps you verify that notifications were received and troubleshoot any delivery issues.

Failed alerts to another system show the reason for failure and how many attempts were made. You can use this information to check your system's configuration or network connectivity.

## Best practices

- Set up alerts for your high-priority vessels first.
- Test email and SMS alerts with a small group before rolling out to your entire team.
- If you use alerts to another system, verify with your IT team that the destination URL is monitored and logged.
- Review your alert history weekly to catch any delivery problems early.
- Adjust quiet hours based on your actual workflow to avoid unnecessary holds.
